hold on to.example: That way, if my mama ever came back, I could recognize her, and I would be able to grab her and hold on to her tight and not let her get away from me again.
hold on to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

i bet.example: “I bet you don’t belong to anybody.”
i bet.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

i guess.meaning: "I guess" means "I think so, but I am not sure."
i guess.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

i mean.meaning: You say it when you want to say something again in a better way.
i mean.example: I mean I have one, but I don’t know where she is.
i mean.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

i'm afraid.meaning: A polite way to say "I'm sorry, but...".
i'm afraid.example: But I’m afraid to ask the preacher; I’m afraid he’ll get mad at me.”
i'm afraid.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in charge of.meaning: Having the job of looking after something or leading others.
in charge of.example: It’s just a little old house full of books, and Miss Franny Block is in charge of them all.
in charge of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in the meantime.meaning: During the time before something happens.
in the meantime.example: But in the meantime, you got to remember, you can’t always judge people by the things they done.
in the meantime.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the middle of.meaning: In the centre of a place, or during an event.
in the middle of.example: were sitting and cocked his head, like he was saying, “What in the world are you two doing out of bed in the middle of the
in the middle of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

instead of.meaning: In the place of something else.
instead of.example: People bring in their own foldup chairs and lawn chairs, and so sometimes it looks more like the congregation is watching a parade or sitting at a barbecue instead of being at church.
instead of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

just in time.meaning: Just before it was too late.
just in time.example: I got the preacher up off the floor and out of the way just in time.
just in time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep an eye on.example: “We’ll have to keep an eye on him,” the preacher said.
keep an eye on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

kind of.example: He was kind of limping like something was wrong with one of his legs.
kind of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

knock out.meaning: To make someone fall asleep or become unconscious.
knock out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

lay off.meaning: (Informal) "Lay off her" = stop bothering or attacking her.
lay off.example: “Oh, lay off her,” Dunlap said to Stevie.
lay off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

like crazy.example: But none of it lasted long, because Winn-Dixie came tearing back out of the preacher’s room, panting and running like crazy.
like crazy.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

look forward to.meaning: To feel happy about something that is going to happen.
look forward to.example: “I been looking forward to it all day.
look forward to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

lose your nerve.meaning: To suddenly feel too afraid to do something you planned to do.
lose your nerve.example: “Daddy,” I said, real quick before I lost all my nerve, “I’ve been talking to Winn-Dixie.”
lose your nerve.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make friends with.meaning: To start to be friends with someone.
make friends with.example: That night when the preacher was tucking me into bed, I told him how I got a job at Gertrude’s Pets, and I told him all about making friends with Miss Franny Block and getting invited to Sweetie Pie’s party, and I told him about meeting Gloria Dump.
make friends with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make fun of.meaning: To laugh at someone in an unkind or teasing way.
make fun of.example: The manager sat up and gave me a hard stare, like maybe I was making fun of him.
make fun of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make head nor tail of.meaning: "Can't make head nor tail of something" = cannot understand it at all. Here it is a joke: she could not cook meat at all.
make head nor tail of.example: She couldn’t make head nor tail of a piece of meat.
make head nor tail of.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

make sure.meaning: To check that something is true or will happen.
make sure.example: “We’ll have to make sure he doesn’t get out during a storm.
make sure.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

me neither.meaning: "Me neither" means "I don't either." You say it to agree with something negative.
me neither.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

mean it.meaning: To say something and really want it to be true. "She meant it" means she was not joking.
mean it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

most certainly.meaning: (Old-fashioned) Very certainly; yes, of course ("He most certainly is a large dog").
most certainly.example: She looked down at him and said, “He most certainly is a large dog.”
most certainly.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

most likely.meaning: Probably. This is what will probably happen.

my goodness.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

never mind.meaning: It does not matter; do not worry about it.
never mind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no wonder.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

not at all.example: And there were bald patches all over him, places where he didn’t have any fur at all.
not at all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

nothing but.example: Back when Florida was wild, when it consisted of nothing but palmetto trees and mosquitoes so big they could fly away with you,” Miss Franny Block started in, “and I was just a little girl no bigger than you, my father, Herman W.
nothing but.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh well.meaning: A thing you say when you accept something bad that you cannot change.
oh well.example: “Oh, well,” said Miss Franny, “perhaps three times the size of your dog.”
oh well.usageNote: Informal spoken English. "Ah, well" means the same. Here "well" does not mean "in a good way".

on account of.example: “It was on account of the music,” he said.
on account of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

on purpose.meaning: Because you want to; not by accident.
on purpose.example: But when he did that, his guitar slid forward and hit him in the head with a little boing sound; Sweetie Pie laughed and pointed at him like he was doing the whole thing on purpose just to amuse her.
on purpose.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

on your own.meaning: Alone, without help from other people.
on your own.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

out loud.meaning: In a voice that other people can hear.
out loud.example: I wrote them down just the way he said them to me so that I wouldn’t forget them, and then I read them out loud to Winn-Dixie until I had them memorized.
out loud.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

out of nowhere.meaning: Suddenly, from no place you can see.
out of nowhere.example: “That came right out of nowhere,” said the preacher.
out of nowhere.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

over and over.example: I kept on going over and over the list in my head.
over and over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pay attention.meaning: To listen or look with care.

peanut butter.meaning: A soft brown food made from peanuts. People put it on bread.
peanut butter.example: “This dog sure likes peanut butter,” she said.
peanut butter.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

pick out.meaning: To choose one thing from a group ("pick out my two tomatoes").
pick out.example: This is what happened: I walked into the produce section of the Winn-Dixie grocery store to pick out my two tomatoes and I almost bumped right into the store manager.
pick out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pinch faced.meaning: Having a face that looks tight and unhappy.
pinch faced.example: Block Memorial Library but old pinch-faced Amanda Wilkinson.

pointy toed.meaning: Having a shoe or boot that comes to a sharp end.
pointy toed.example: He was playing a guitar and he had on skinny pointy-toed cowboy boots and he was tapping them while he was playing the music.

read aloud.meaning: To read words in a voice that other people can hear.
read aloud.example: It’s been a tradition in my family to read the book aloud.
read aloud.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

remind someone of.meaning: To make someone think of something similar.
remind someone of.example: Sometimes he reminded me of a turtle hiding inside its shell, in there thinking about things and not ever sticking his head out into the world.
remind someone of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

right away.example: “You are a suffering dog, so maybe he will take to you right away.
right away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

roll your eyes.meaning: To move your eyes up to show you think something is stupid or boring.
roll your eyes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

root beer.example: It tasted like root beer and strawberry and something else I didn’t have a name for, something that made me feel kind of sad.

run into.example: I grabbed the platter of egg-salad sandwiches and the preacher grabbed the punch, and we ran into the kitchen with them; and when I ran back outside, I saw that Amanda had hold of Miss Franny Block and was helping her into the house.
run into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sense of humor.meaning: The ability to laugh at things and make others laugh.
sense of humor.example: It’s hard not to immediately fall in love with a dog who has a good sense of humor.
sense of humor.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

set up.meaning: To get a machine ready to use.
set up.example: But I love this collar and leash, and so does my dog, and I was thinking that maybe you could set me up on an installment plan.”
set up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

shake your head.meaning: To move your head from side to side to say "no" or to show you are unhappy.
shake your head.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

show up.example: I promised that I would, and then I introduced Sweetie Pie to Miss Franny and to Gloria, and right after that, the preacher showed up.
show up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

shut up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

side by side.example: But when I reread Because of Winn-Dixie in preparation for this anniversary edition, I found it painful to see Opal and Gloria Dump sitting together, side by side, reading from a book that I cannot in good conscience recommend to my readers.
side by side.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

smarty pants.meaning: (Informal) Someone who acts as if they know everything.
smarty pants.example: I was a miss-smarty-pants with my library full of books.
smarty pants.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sore loser.meaning: Someone who gets angry or upset when they lose a game.
sore loser.example: I told him he was just a sore loser.”
sore loser.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

speaking of.meaning: Used when you want to say more about something that was just talked about.
speaking of.example: Speaking of perfection, no book is ever perfect, and there are certainly more things that could be changed in Because of Winn-Dixie.
speaking of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stick together.meaning: Stay together and help each other.
stick together.example: I used my own hairbrush and worked real hard at all the knots and patches of fur stuck together.
stick together.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

suit yourself.meaning: Do what you want. (Said when you are a bit annoyed.)
suit yourself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

sure enough.example: And sure enough, standing there on the sidewalk was Otis.
sure enough.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

take care of.meaning: To look after someone or something.
take care of.example: You could still see his ribs, but I intended to feed him good and that would take care of that.
take care of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

teddy bear.example: She sat on the floor and wrapped her arms around Winn-Dixie and rocked him back and forth like he was a big old teddy bear.
teddy bear.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

tell on.meaning: (Informal) To tell a teacher or parent that someone did something wrong.
tell on.example: And none of them wanted to be my friend anyway because they probably thought I’d tell on them to the preacher for every little thing they did wrong; and then they would get in trouble with God and their parents.
tell on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the rest of.example: I wanted to hear the rest of the story.
the rest of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

turn out.meaning: To happen or to be a certain way in the end ("turned out fine").
turn out.example: Winn-Dixie hopped up on the bed, and the preacher got up and turned out the light.
turn out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

used to.meaning: Did something regularly in the past, but not now. "Be used to" = know something well, so it is not strange.
used to.example: The building used to be a Pick-It-Quick store, and when you walk in the front door, the first thing you see is the Pick-It-Quick motto.
used to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

wait a minute.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

watch out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

wear out.meaning: To make someone very tired ("wore me out"). "Wore out" (spoken) = worn out, very tired.
wear out.example: I swear, it about wore me out yelling at Dunlap and Stevie Dewberry every day; by the time I got to Gloria Dump’s yard, I felt like a soldier who had been fighting a hard battle.
wear out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

what's going on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

with all my heart.meaning: Very, very much; with all my love.
with all my heart.example: He was an ugly dog, but already, I loved him with all my heart.
with all my heart.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

yes indeed.meaning: (Old-fashioned) "Yes, indeed" = yes, certainly; that is very true.
yes indeed.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

yes ma'am.meaning: (Southern US, polite) "Yes, madam." Children in the South say "ma'am" to women to be polite. "No ma'am" = no, madam. Miss Franny says "Yes ma'am" just to make what she says stronger.
yes ma'am.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

you bet.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

you know what.meaning: "You know what?" is a way to start telling someone something interesting.
you know what.example: “But you know what?” I told Winn-Dixie.
you know what.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

you're welcome.meaning: What you say when someone thanks you.
you're welcome.example: “Child,” she said, “as long as this is my garden, you’re welcome in it.
you're welcome.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.
